passage: Akash, sit with your Jasleen Bua. Your heart is racing before the board exam, and you think it means something terrible will happen. At your age I thought the same. The night before my Class 10 exams my chest thumped and I was sure I'd fail. My Biji didn't say "relax". She said, "The drum is telling you to slow down, not that the sky is falling." We walked twice round the gurdwara compound, I told her every worry out loud, and then I slept. Later, in college, when the worry stopped me sleeping for weeks, Biji was the one who said, "Now we see a doctor who knows about minds." That helped too. So, puttar, walk with me, tell me the worries, and then bed.

qa.q: What did Biji say the drum was telling young Jasleen?
qa.a: To slow down, not that the sky is falling.

qa.q: How does Akash seem to feel about his racing heart before the exam?
qa.a: He seems frightened, thinking the racing heart means something terrible will happen in the exam.

qa.q: What steps did Biji use the night before Jasleen's exams?
qa.a: They walked twice round the compound, Jasleen said every worry aloud, and then slept.

qa.q: How might Biji have seen young Jasleen's thumping chest that night?
qa.a: Biji seems to have seen it as a signal to slow down, not a disaster, and trusted that walking and talking would settle the worry.

grounding: An aunt shows her nephew how to read big feelings as signals to slow down, using movement, naming worries, sleep and, when it persists, a professional.

passage: The bus to the state quiz final broke down on the highway, and Abhinav's team arrived with eight minutes to spare, into a hall packed with noise. His heart started hammering. The old thought came: something is wrong. Then the newer one: this is a signal to slow down, not proof. He walked once up and down the corridor, fast, shaking out his hands. "Vaibhav," he said to his teammate, "I'm nervous. Like, a lot." Vaibhav bumped his shoulder. "Same. Take the science round?" Abhinav nodded. Last term, when the worry had kept him awake for weeks, he had told his parents, and they had found a counsellor he still saw on Thursdays. Tonight he would sleep. Right now, he would answer.

qa.q: How many minutes to spare did the team have when they arrived?
qa.a: They arrived with eight minutes to spare.

qa.q: What was Abhinav thinking when his heart started hammering?
qa.a: First the old thought that something was wrong, then the newer one that it was a signal to slow down, not proof.

qa.q: Which steps did Abhinav take before the quiz, and why did they help?
qa.a: He walked the corridor shaking out his hands and told Vaibhav he was nervous, which steadied him enough to play.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have felt when Abhinav admitted being nervous?
qa.a: Vaibhav seems relieved to share it, answering "Same", and the honesty makes both feel less alone.

grounding: Under a stressful delay, a teenager treats his racing heart as a signal to slow down, moves, names his worry to a teammate, and keeps seeing a counsellor.

passage: Ten minutes before the inter-school debate final in the Jaipur auditorium, Binita's heart started hammering and her hands went cold. The old Binita would have taken it as proof: something is wrong, I'll blank, I should leave. This time she told herself plainly: this is my body getting ready, not danger. Slow down. She walked the corridor twice, breathing out longer than in. Then she found Gurleen by the water cooler. 'I'm scared I'll forget my rebuttal,' she said. Saying it made it smaller. Gurleen squeezed her arm. 'You've got your cards. And you slept this time.' She had, on purpose. Last year the worry had not switched off for months, and the school counsellor had helped her build these habits. Binita walked on stage. Her voice shook for one line, then steadied.

qa.q: What did Binita do in the corridor?
qa.a: She walked it twice, breathing out longer than in.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling ten minutes before the final?
qa.a: She felt scared, heart hammering and hands cold, worried she would forget her rebuttal.

qa.q: Which habits helped Binita, and where did they come from?
qa.a: Reading her racing heart as a signal to slow down, walking, naming the worry to Gurleen and sleeping well; she built them with the school counsellor when the worry wouldn't switch off.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Binita's words by the water cooler?
qa.a: Gurleen seems glad to be trusted with the worry, and answers with calm, practical reassurance.

grounding: Shows a teenager who treats a surge of fear as a signal to slow down, using movement, sleep, naming the worry and a trusted friend, after earlier professional help.

passage:
'Nikita? It's past eleven.' Gautam stood in the doorway.
'I can't sleep, Papa. What if I blank in the chemistry exam? What if everyone else gets science and I don't?'
He came and sat on the chair. 'That's a big worry. Where do you feel it?'
'Chest. Tight.'
'Okay. That tightness is a signal to slow down, not proof the worst will happen. Try this: write every what-if on this page, then close the notebook.'
She wrote four. He read them without laughing.
'Tomorrow, before school, walk with me to the milk booth. Moving helps.'
'That's it?'
'Not quite. You've had this tight chest most nights for a month now. That's too long to carry alone. On Saturday we'll talk to the school counsellor, together.'
Nikita looked at the closed notebook. 'Okay.' Her shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: Where does Nikita feel the worry?
qa.a: In her chest, which feels tight.

qa.q: What was Nikita worried about?
qa.a: She was anxious that she would blank in the chemistry exam and not get science.

qa.q: Which of Gautam's steps help tonight, and which address the longer pattern?
qa.a: Writing down the what-ifs and a morning walk help tonight; seeing the school counsellor on Saturday addresses a worry that has lasted a month.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel reading her four what-ifs?
qa.a: He was probably worried but calm, reading them seriously without laughing so that she felt heard.

grounding: Shows a parent helping a teenager treat worry as a signal to slow down, with writing, movement and sleep, and arranging professional help for distress that has persisted.

passage: The spring before my college entrance exams, my worries grew teeth. I'm Keerthana. I'd wake at three with my heart racing, sure I had already failed. What helped in the end wasn't one big thing. It was small ones. My Rukmini Paati made me walk with her to the temple tank every evening, no phone. I started going to bed at the same time. When my chest tightened, I'd say the worry out loud, 'I'm scared I'll let Appa down,' and it shrank a little just by being said. I told Paati everything on those walks. But after some weeks the three o'clock waking still hadn't stopped, and Paati said gently, 'This needs someone who knows more than me.' Appa took me to a counsellor. I went every week until the exams. The worry didn't vanish. It just stopped driving.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini Paati walk with Keerthana?
qa.a: To the temple tank every evening.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when waking at three?
qa.a: Keerthana felt panicky and afraid, heart racing, sure of having already failed.

qa.q: Why was Paati right to suggest a counsellor?
qa.a: The walks and routines helped, but when the night waking kept going, the distress needed someone with more training.

qa.q: What might Rukmini Paati have felt on those evening walks?
qa.a: Paati probably felt worried but steady, listening closely, and cared enough to admit when more help was needed.

grounding: Shows a teenager managing an anxious temperament with movement, sleep, naming worries and a trusted grandparent, and seeing a counsellor when the distress persists.

passage:
Coach's notebook, district relay week.
Aadhya came to practice on Tuesday pale and quiet. "My heart's going crazy. What if I drop the baton again?" she said. Last year she did, once.
I didn't tell her it was nothing. I said, "Your heart's telling you this matters. It's a signal to slow down, not a sign you'll fail." We walked one easy lap while she named three worries out loud. Ankita, her partner on the handover, listened and said, "I worry about that too."
We made a small plan: an early night before the meet, a short jog in the morning, and ten slow handovers with Ankita instead of fifty fast ones.
She ran well on Saturday, still shaky at the start line.
Afterwards she told me the worry follows her at home too, most nights. I thanked her for telling me, and with her permission I called her mother that evening so they could talk to the school counsellor together.

qa.q: How many slow handovers did Aadhya plan to practise with Ankita?
qa.a: Ten slow handovers.

qa.q: What was Aadhya worried about on Tuesday?
qa.a: She felt anxious that she might drop the baton again; she was pale and quiet and said her heart was going crazy.

qa.q: What did the coach do well when Aadhya said the worry follows her most nights?
qa.a: The coach thanked her and, with her permission, called her mother that same evening so they could talk to the school counsellor together, since ongoing worry deserves more support.

qa.q: How might Ankita's words have affected Aadhya?
qa.a: Hearing "I worry about that too" from her handover partner likely made Aadhya feel less alone and less ashamed of her nerves.

grounding: Shows a coach helping a teen treat racing nerves as a signal, using sleep, movement, naming worries and sharing, and involving a counsellor for ongoing distress.
